target_customer: High volume delivery restaurants (pizza and similar) that wanted outsourced drivers, plus independent drivers who took the shifts
problem: Restaurants with heavy delivery volume struggled to staff and manage their own drivers. Zoomer supplied a driver network and dispatch platform so restaurants could deliver faster and more consistently.
business_model: B2B logistics: per delivery fees charged to restaurants, with independent drivers paid per delivery

founders.name: Justin Goldman
founders.background_notes: Listed as Founder and CEO on the YC page. No background found in sources opened.

founders.name: Vasanth Elavarasan
founders.background_notes: Listed as founder on the YC page. No background found.

founders.name: Robert Shedd
founders.background_notes: Listed as Founder and CTO on the YC page. No background found.

exit.reason: A letter to Lexington, Kentucky restaurants cited local delivery competition (UberEats, GrubHub and others) and independent contractor competition. EatStreet took over certain assets, about 30 employees and contracts in 10 markets; Zoomer technology was reportedly not part of the transfer.

competitors.name: DoorDash
competitors.what: Delivery from local restaurants using its own driver fleet and logistics, launching in the San Jose area
competitors.traction_then: Launched in San Jose in January 2014 after YC S13

technical_complexity.rationale: Real time dispatch for a very high volume of concurrent deliveries is a standard but non trivial logistics problem, and the company described its platform as built for that load.

defensibility.rationale: Independent driver supply and restaurant contracts were replicable by better funded delivery platforms. No data or network effect moat is evidenced.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Competition from larger delivery platforms and contractor competition was cited in the January 2017 closing letter. EatStreet took over assets and part of the workforce.

market_need_then: Restaurant delivery was growing and restaurants with high volume had driver staffing problems. The company's own description says it was growing its restaurant, driver and diner base, but no independent figures were found.

branding.domain_note: Company site was zoomerdelivery.com per the YC description, a descriptive suffix domain rather than the exact .com. The site did not resolve when fetched.

identity.voice_and_tone: Upbeat startup recruiting copy (wow customers, up and to the right)

brand_strength.rationale: The company said it stayed out of the spotlight. Searches found no press on the brand itself and the name collides with several other Zoomer and Zoom delivery names.

outcome_analysis: Zoomer grew to about 51 people across several markets as a B2B driver network for high volume delivery restaurants, but the 2017 closing letter blamed competition from UberEats, GrubHub and independent contractors. It shut down in January 2017 after a sudden email to drivers and restaurants, and EatStreet took some contracts, drivers and staff. The cause is partly inferred from the letter; unit economics and fundraising failure are not stated by the company and rest on the pattern of the shutdown.
notes: The $120K total raised rests on a single database (CB Insights) and is probably the YC deal; it omits Foundation Capital, which the company's own description lists with SV Angel and Eric Ries. Technical.ly did not give amounts. Technical.ly said the EatStreet deal was unconfirmed at publication; Philly Mag later reported the partial acquisition. Failure factors unit_economics and could_not_raise_next_round are inferred and not stated by the company. The company site zoomerdelivery.com did not resolve when fetched.
